title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 109: The Saffron Crocus: The Golden Spice
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 109 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Saffron Crocus: The Golden Spice

Paragraph 1. Produced from the delicate red stigmas of Crocus sativus, saffron has long been famous as the world's most expensive spice by weight. Known historically as 'vegetable gold', it has shaped cooking, medicine, and royal traditions across three continents for over three thousand years. Unlike its wild ancestors, the farmed saffron plant is sterile; it cannot produce seeds or spread on its own in nature. Its survival depends completely on farmers digging up and separating underground storage bulbs called corms and planting them by hand.

Paragraph 2. The extremely high cost of saffron comes directly from its difficult harvest. Each purple flower holds only three slender stigmas, which must be plucked carefully from the open bloom. All harvesting happens within a short two-to-three-week window in late autumn. Because flowers open at dawn and quickly fade as temperatures rise, field workers must finish picking every flower before sunrise. Waiting until midday allows sunlight to break down delicate oils and lower quality. Producing just one kilogram of dry saffron takes 150,000 to 200,000 blossoms and forty hours of hard manual work.

Paragraph 3. Archaeological evidence proves that saffron farming began during the Bronze Age. Colourful wall paintings called frescoes, uncovered at Akrotiri on the island of Santorini, show young women gathering saffron blossoms into woven baskets. In ancient Rome, people used saffron essence as perfume inside public baths and scattered it over stone arenas to cover unpleasant smells, while wealthy brides wore bright yellow saffron veils.

Paragraph 4. During the Middle Ages, saffron often cost more than pure gold, encouraging widespread cheating among merchants. Dishonest traders soaked batches in honey or oil to make shipments heavier, or mixed in cheap marigold petals and dyed silk. In response, European cities passed strict laws. In Nuremberg, Germany, inspectors tested every batch entering the city, and merchants found guilty of selling fake saffron were burned at the stake or buried alive.

Paragraph 5. Even today, machines have failed to replace hand-picking. Iran produces over eighty-five percent of global saffron across its dry northeastern provinces. Saffron's unique qualities come from three main chemicals: crocin provides its golden-yellow colour, picrocrocin gives its bitter flavour, and safranal creates its pleasant aroma. However, climate scientists warn that changing rainfall patterns and unexpected frosts now threaten traditional planting schedules.

groups.title: Questions 6–10
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

steps: Đoạn 3: "...used saffron essence as perfume inside public baths..."

q6.text: Wall paintings at Akrotiri show older men supervising young saffron pickers.

steps: Đoạn 3: Bích họa chỉ vẽ phụ nữ trẻ hái hoa (young women gathering saffron blossoms), không có đàn ông lớn tuổi giám sát.

q7.text: Medieval traders sometimes mixed saffron with honey to increase its weight.

steps: Đoạn 4: "Dishonest traders soaked batches in honey or oil to make shipments heavier..."

q8.text: Merchants caught cheating in Nuremberg could avoid death by paying financial fines.

steps: Đoạn 4: Thương nhân gian lận bị thiêu sống hoặc chôn sống (burned at the stake or buried alive), không được nộp phạt thoát tội.

q9.text: Crocin is the chemical compound that creates saffron's strong aroma.

steps: Đoạn 5: Crocin tạo màu vàng óng, còn safranal mới là chất tạo mùi thơm.

q10.text: Farmers in northeastern Iran receive government money to protect corms from frost.

steps: Đoạn 5: Bài có nhắc sương giá đe dọa mùa vụ ở Iran nhưng không đề cập chính phủ có hỗ trợ tiền hay không.
